turns.t: Doctor, I'm precise, so listen. My daughter Lily, she's five, pushed a bead into her left ear this morning at eight forty. She says it hurts.
It doesn't hurt.
Lily, you said it hurt, you were crying.
Hello Lily. Does your ear hurt now, sweetheart?
No. It's just there.
I'll note that you say it doesn't hurt, and Mum says you were crying. What was the bead like?
Small, round, red plastic, from her craft box. About five millimetres. ~
Did anything come out of the ear?
No blood, no fluid.
Has she had any ear problems before? ~
No, never. ~
Is she on any medicines?
A teaspoon of something, I think. Calpol, maybe, five mil, at breakfast, because I was worried.
Thank you. How long ago? ~
It's now ten-thirty, so about two hours. ~
Lily, I'm going to look in your ear with a torch. You must keep very still. Can you do that for me? ~
Okay.
I can see a small red bead in the outer part of the ear canal, and the skin around it is a little pink, but there's no bleeding, and I can't see the eardrum behind it. ~
Can you get it out? ~
I'd like to try. I'll use a small hook, and a gentle suction. It takes a few minutes, and she must stay still. Mum, will you hold her on your lap?
Yes. Of course. ~
Lily, you're going to hear a funny noise.
Got it. Here it is. ~
Can I see? ~
Yes, look. A little red bead. ~
Oh, thank goodness. ~
I'll check the ear again, to make sure there's no scratch.
The ear canal has a tiny graze at the entrance, but the eardrum looks normal, and there's no damage. ~
Will she need antibiotics? ~
No. Don't put anything in the ear, keep it dry for a couple of days, and don't let her poke at it.
Right. ~
If she gets earache, discharge, or says she can't hear, bring her back.
Understood. ~
And a word to keep the craft beads out of reach, and teach her to tell you if she puts something in. ~
I will. Thank you so much, doctor. ~
Bye bye. ~
